items.title: Passive central banks make rate risk THE variable into FOMC
items.idea: Capital Flows argues the entire institutional/wealth stack is long stocks and bonds with no playbook for a 2022-style joint selloff. France is the live case: investors forced to sell both equities and bonds, so stocks fall as yields rise. The claim is that ALL the debt sits on government balance sheets, and the French episode is a preview of a US version 'in a different form'.
items.angle: Stock-bond correlation regime is the book's real risk factor; ties to covariance trades and duration hedges rather than directional equity views.
items.tweetA: Everyone has a 60/40 playbook for recession. Nobody has one for 'stocks and bonds fall together because the sovereign is the problem'. France is running that experiment live. Who's your hedge when the diversifier is the thing breaking?
items.tweetB: Rate vol isn't a bond-desk problem anymore. If a passive central bank means the curve does the adjusting, every equity multiple is a duration instrument. Price your book in DV01, not sectors.

items.title: Elice -32% on Seoul debut: the AI trade stops being a monolith
items.idea: South Korean AI-computing supplier Elice fell 32% on its first day while CoreWeave stays volatile on leverage and financing worries. The author's read: phase one of a theme is exposure, phase two is hierarchy - sorting by who can fund themselves, convert capex to earnings, or needs generous capital markets.
items.angle: IPO window for AI compute is now discriminating; short-the-weak-balance-sheet / long-the-self-funded is the pair, not long-AI.
items.tweetA: A -32% debut for an AI compute name in the same week SpaceX prints $4.4B of net income. That's not an AI bust, it's a sorting mechanism. Phase two of every theme is 'who pays for their own capex'.
items.tweetB: Pair idea: self-funded AI (cash flow covers capex) vs levered compute rentals. The Elice and CoreWeave tape says the market already runs this trade. The question is how many other IPOs are queued behind Elice.

items.title: Brent ~$109 while US-Iran talks set the macro backdrop
items.idea: The Asia-open note mentions Brent settled near $109 as traders parse US-Iran negotiation headlines, long Treasuries outperformed, and 400+ S&P 500 names closed higher. The author treats oil as backdrop rather than driver.
items.angle: $109 Brent plus a long-bond bid is a stagflation-fear signature, not a growth one; keep oil as a macro input into rate paths.
items.tweetA: Brent at $109, long bonds outperforming, 400+ S&P names green. Pick the odd one out. Either oil is wrong or the bond market is pricing the demand destruction.
items.tweetB: Equities treating $109 oil as 'backdrop' is the tell. Last time crude sat here the Fed was the story. This time the story is a negotiation headline away from $90 or $130. $XLE $USO

items.title: SpaceX's AI unit ($7.56B) is now bigger than Starlink ($5.25B) and profitable
items.idea: SpaceX Q3: revenue $14.58B vs $12.87B est, adj. EBITDA $8.81B vs $6.59B, net income $4.4B vs $1.88B. Super Intelligence revenue $7.56B overtook Starlink's $5.25B; the AI unit swung from a $1.26B operating loss to a $431M profit. Cursor contributed $608M between August close and quarter-end.
items.angle: AI monetisation debate got a hard datapoint from an unexpected name. Read-through to Nvidia demand and to every 'where's the revenue' bear thesis.
items.tweetA: A rocket company just reported more AI revenue than satellite revenue. $7.56B vs $5.25B, and the AI unit went from -$1.26B to +$431M operating income in one quarter. Please update the 'no AI revenue' slide.
items.tweetB: Cursor added $608M in roughly two months after the acquisition closed. At that run rate a coding tool is a $3-4B annualised business inside a rocket company. I did not have that on my 2026 bingo card. $NVDA

items.title: $19.59B of quarterly capex: even the winner is a capital-allocation story
items.idea: SpaceX spent $19.59B capex in the quarter and is exploring more financing to buy Nvidia chips. Cash was $51.3B vs ~$91B expected, but $38.6B of marketable securities restored ~$90B liquidity. The roughly $2T valuation already prices Starlink, Super Intelligence, Starship and orbital data centres.
items.angle: The test is no longer demand but return on the next dollar; relevant for sizing hyperscaler and neocloud exposure by funding cost.
items.tweetA: $19.6B of capex in ninety days from a company that just beat EBITDA by 34%. If the cleanest AI balance sheet still needs outside financing for chips, what does the median neocloud look like? $CRWV
items.tweetB: The market marked down a 'cash miss' of $40B that was just classification. That's how sensitive the AI complex is to liquidity optics now. Next quarter's tell isn't revenue, it's the cost of the debt that funds the GPUs.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Starlink: 13.6M consumer subs (from 12M) and V3 via Starship
items.idea: Starlink consumer subscribers rose to 13.6M from 12M in a quarter (+13%), connectivity revenue to $5.25B from $4.29B (+22%), with the higher-capacity V3 network beginning to roll out via Starship. Enterprise/government demand and profitability improving.
items.angle: Satellite broadband is a utility-like cash engine funding the AI bet; watch telecom and rural-broadband read-through.
items.tweetA: 1.6M new Starlink subscribers in one quarter. That's a mid-size cable operator's worth of customers added every 90 days, with no trenching permit required.
items.tweetB: Starlink revenue +22% QoQ and V3 only just starting to ship via Starship. The boring connectivity business is subsidising the capex-hungry AI bet, and nobody models it as a utility.

items.title: Washington's $25M whistleblower fund pays only for convictions
items.idea: Trump and Vance announced a $25M fund paying up to $30,000 per tip, but only if tips 'lead to federal convictions' - run by DOJ. Fulcrum's point: this selects for prosecutable cases (like last week's 76-defendant, $490M tax enforcement surge) over system-failure disclosures, and $30k is small versus a whistleblower's career risk. Treasury flagged ~$270M of suspicious student-aid activity that would not qualify without a conviction.
items.angle: Incentive design signal; contrasts with False Claims Act civil relators who share recoveries. Relevant to government contractors and benefits-program exposure.
items.tweetA: $30k max reward, paid only on conviction. The False Claims Act gives relators a percentage of recoveries and that's why it actually works. This is a bounty designed to look good in a press release.
items.tweetB: Look at what it doesn't pay for: control failures, duplicate-identity databases, procurement waivers. The expensive government losses are the ones with no defendant. So the fund will measure prosecutor convenience and call it fraud detection.

items.title: Netflix sells off as it concedes slowing viewership growth
items.idea: In the 'Things happen' section: Netflix acknowledged investor concern about slowing viewership growth and intense competition, pledged to revive viewing trends, and the stock sold off. Paired in the same issue with SpaceX reporting 161% revenue growth.
items.angle: Dispersion-in-earnings theme: the market pays for growth and punishes decelerating engagement even in quality names.
items.tweetA: SpaceX +161% revenue, Netflix sold for admitting viewing time is flattening. Same evening, same market. The bar isn't 'good company', it's 'is the growth rate still accelerating'. $NFLX
items.tweetB: Netflix is competing with YouTube, short video and now AI-generated feeds for the same hours. A pledge to 'revive viewing trends' is an admission that engagement, not subscribers, is the constraint. That's a different valuation framework.

items.title: GDPNow 3.5% vs NY Fed 2.7%; Q3 started at +6.2%
items.idea: Atlanta Fed GDPNow for Q3 is +3.5% (peaked 6.2% early in the quarter), NY Fed Nowcast +2.7%. Q1 was revised to 2.5% from 2.1% and Q2 to 2.2% from 1.5% annualised. Both Q3 nowcasts sit above the ~2.1% potential growth estimate.
items.angle: Growth is not the constraint on the Fed; supports a higher-for-longer rate path and the stock-bond correlation risk in other items.
items.tweetA: Two Fed nowcasts, 3.5% and 2.7%, and the gap between them is bigger than the gap to potential. The upside surprise in growth is the thing the curve isn't priced for.
items.tweetB: Q2 got revised from 1.5% to 2.2% after the fact. Every cycle call made on the first print was wrong by 70bps. Be careful anchoring on advance GDP.

items.title: Underlying growth: final sales to private domestic purchasers jumped to 4.6% from 1.8%
items.idea: Stripping out government spending, net trade and inventories, real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose to 4.6% annualised in Q2 2026 from 1.8% in Q1 while headline Q2 was 2.2%. Mav calls it a 'very good reading'.
items.angle: The headline/underlying gap says private demand is much stronger than GDP shows - the drag was in government and trade lines.
items.tweetA: Headline Q2 GDP 2.2%. Private final demand 4.6%. The gap is government, trade and inventories. The private economy is running at twice the number everyone quotes.
items.tweetB: If core private demand is at 4.6% and oil is ~$109, the Fed isn't cutting its way out of anything. Which part of the market is priced for a 4.6% economy? I can't find it.

items.title: Dallas Fed Weekly Economic Index: 3.05%, 13-week average 2.91%
items.idea: The WEI, scaled to y/y GDP growth, read 3.05% for the week ended Oct 10 (2.68% prior week), with the 13-week MA at 2.91%, above the 2.06% potential-growth line and above the 2.19% official Q2 rate. Mav reads it as accelerating growth.
items.angle: A high-frequency cross-check on nowcasts; three independent real-time gauges point above trend.
items.tweetA: Atlanta Fed, NY Fed and Dallas Fed weekly index all above potential. When three independent real-time gauges agree, that isn't noise.
items.tweetB: WEI 2.91% on a 13-week smooth vs 2.19% official Q2. The weekly data is leading the quarterly print by about 70bps. That's the number to watch before the next FOMC.

items.title: Presidential net job approval -22.4% (Silver Bulletin) / -21.1% (RCP) despite solid growth
items.idea: Net approval has been negative since mid-March 2025 (Trade War 2.0) and now sits at -22.4% on Silver Bulletin and -21.1% on Real Clear Politics. Mav's takeaway: if the economy is doing well and approval is this low, weaker growth would produce an even bigger drop.
items.angle: Midterms are weeks away (per ARD); approval-vs-growth disconnect points to prices/affordability or non-economic drivers.
items.tweetA: Net approval -22 with GDP tracking 3.5%. The economy is the best card the incumbent has and it still isn't working. Maybe the problem is the price level, not the growth rate.
items.tweetB: A -22 net rating with a strong nowcast is the cleanest 'vibecession' datapoint I can think of. Markets are pricing policy continuity into the midterms. That's a position, not a base case.

items.title: OpenAI: COBOL coding 11% to 72%, migration 5% to 87% (98% with more effort)
items.idea: OpenAI says its newest model passed ~87% of a build-a-SQLite-compatible-database test across 20 languages vs ~27% for the previous model; COBOL 11% to 72%, Fortran 21% to 84%. On migrating COBOL programs without changing behavior: 87% vs 5%, and 98% with more effort. COBOL still underpins 40%+ of online banking, 80% of in-person card payments and 95% of ATM transactions.
items.angle: Legacy modernisation is the clearest enterprise AI ROI case; negative for COBOL-services labor moats, positive for banks' tech cost structure.
items.tweetA: COBOL runs 95% of ATM transactions and migration accuracy just went from 5% to 87%. The Y2K labour shortage that kept the mainframe moat alive is closing. $IBM $ACN
items.tweetB: Every bank has a decade-long mainframe migration on the roadmap that nobody dared start. At 98% with more compute, the question flips from 'can we' to 'why are we still paying'. Who loses: consultancies, not banks.

items.title: DHS orders federal agencies to purge DeepSeek and anything built on it
items.idea: DHS ordered civilian federal agencies to remove DeepSeek AI, bars future purchases, and extends to affiliates and other companies' products built on its models, using a 2018 supply-chain security law with no specific security concern or deadline stated. A day later DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer, its production inference software, aimed at cutting compute and energy cost; no independent tests yet.
items.angle: Reaches beyond an app into open weights lineage; compliance headache for vendors embedding Chinese-derived models.
items.tweetA: The ban covers 'products built on its models'. Open weights have no borders, so the compliance question becomes lineage: every vendor needs to prove what's under the hood.
items.tweetB: The US bans DeepSeek on Monday, DeepSeek open-sources its inference stack on Tuesday. One side is restricting access to a technology; the other is publishing the cost curve. Guess which strategy scales.

items.title: Goldman: data-center power demand +170% by 2030; grid queue 2,600 GW, 86 projects cancelled or delayed
items.idea: Goldman sees global data center power demand up 170% from 2025 to 2030 with 60%+ of growth in the US. The interconnection queue holds ~2,600 GW (more than double all US capacity), typical project takes ~5 years; 86 data center projects cancelled or delayed since January, 76 due to local opposition. Nearly $8T of data center spend through 2031, utilities >$1T, hyperscaler debt issuance up to $420B next year (+60%). Parekh adds 1 GW of AI compute costs over $50B and takes 2-3 years.
items.angle: Local opposition has become bipartisan ahead of midterms: power, permits and politics are the bottleneck, not chips.
items.tweetA: 2,600 GW in the queue vs ~1,300 GW built. 76 of 86 cancelled projects died to local opposition, not to the grid. The AI bottleneck isn't electrons, it's county commissions.
items.tweetB: $50B per gigawatt and a five-year interconnect. That's the real moat: whoever already has a permitted site with power. Capex doesn't buy time. $VST $CEG

items.title: Bill Gross turns Idealab's playbook into Idealab.ai: 1.2M business ideas, free
items.idea: Gross's free platform is trained on news, research, patents and company filings and offers over 1.2 million startup ideas each with a starter plan; partners include Imperial College London, Caltech, ASU, Cloudflare and Endeavor. Idealab itself has launched 175+ companies. Parekh recalls GoTo.com (the keyword-auction idea behind Google search ads) started on one of Gross's spreadsheets.
items.angle: If idea generation is free, execution and distribution are the only scarce inputs; relevant to venture supply and seed saturation.
items.tweetA: 1.2 million business ideas, free. Ideas were never the bottleneck, and now they're not even scarce in theory. The scarce thing is a distribution channel and the nerve to ship.
items.tweetB: GoTo.com started as a row in Bill Gross's spreadsheet. Now the spreadsheet has 1.2M rows and anyone can open it. The next startup wave won't be short of ideas; it will be short of buyers.

items.title: Claude Code is being used to de-ad smart TVs: CleanYourTV hits 10k stars, 107 TV models, 37 brands
items.idea: Vibecoding trend: use ADB on Android/Google TVs, let Claude Code enumerate apps/services, disable bloat and install a clean launcher. Ryan Doyle's post got 4.3M views; Gathin's version ~7M views and became CleanYourTV (10,000+ GitHub stars). One Sony Bravia with 2GB RAM went from 42MB free to cutting 15 packages and app memory 1.13GB to 911MB. Risks: some Google TV/Chromecast devices enter a restart loop when the stock launcher is disabled.
items.angle: Consumer adoption signal for agentic coding on hardware the user doesn't own the software of; pressure on ad-subsidised TV platform economics.
items.tweetA: Smart TV makers sell the hardware at a loss and earn on ads. A free repo that disables them in one prompt is a margin attack. 107 models, 37 brands, 10k stars in days. $ROKU
items.tweetB: People are handing a coding agent root-ish access to their parents' TV because the ads were annoying enough. That's the actual adoption curve of agents: not enterprise pilots, but irritation.

items.title: Homebuilders: BLDR -74% and DFH -78% from highs; XHB at fresh 52-week lows
items.idea: XHB made new 52-week lows in recent days. BLDR was +225% at the March 2024 peak vs end-2022 and is now -16.4% since end-2022 (drawdown -74%); DFH peaked +405% and is now only +10.5% (drawdown -78%). SharkNinja (SN) is XHB's largest weight, +110% in a year at all-time highs. Bespoke ties the pain to rates and weak starts and pending sales.
items.angle: Housing is the rate-sensitive canary; a full round-trip suggests rates must fall before a bottom. Appliance strength inside a housing ETF is a composition quirk.
items.tweetA: BLDR and DFH gave back 100% of the post-2022 rally. When a cycle's winners fully round-trip, the question isn't valuation; it's whether the rate regime changed for good.
items.tweetB: The largest weight in the homebuilder ETF is a blender company. XHB hitting lows while SN is at all-time highs tells you what the ETF is actually holding. Check what you own before you call it a housing hedge. $XHB $SN

items.title: Cyprus is no longer 0%: flat 8% on crypto disposals from Jan 1, 2026
items.idea: Outdated 'zero-tax crypto' lists still include Cyprus, but from 1 Jan 2026 qualifying crypto disposals (sales, crypto-to-crypto swaps, spending, gifts giving rise to gains) face a flat 8% income tax. Losses offset only same-year crypto gains of the same person and cannot be carried forward; mined crypto sits outside the regime.
items.angle: Tax-residency arbitrage is shrinking: even the classic havens are moving to a low flat rate rather than zero.
items.tweetA: Cyprus quietly went from 0% to 8% on crypto in 2026, and half the 'move abroad' guides still list it as tax-free. The haven playbook is ageing faster than the Telegram groups recommending it.
items.tweetB: No loss carry-forward plus swaps counted as disposals is the real sting at 8%. An 8% rate on a active DeFi book can cost more than a 20% rate on a buy-and-hold. Read the base, not the headline.

items.title: Classification beats rate: investor vs trader vs business decides your crypto tax
items.idea: The piece compares regimes: Switzerland (private gains exempt, but wealth tax on holdings), Germany (tax-free after >1 year, €1,000 annual threshold), Portugal (365-day exclusion, otherwise 28%), Luxembourg (6-month rule, €500), Malta (token type matters), UAE (AED 1M turnover test for business), Singapore and Hong Kong (no capital gains tax, but trading income taxed). Author adds a flag: high risk Germany changes its 0% rule.
items.angle: For DeFi-heavy books, income/reward tokens and activity classification dominate; a framework for client conversations on domicile.
items.tweetA: 'Where is crypto tax 0%?' is the wrong question. Switzerland taxes your wealth even in years you sell nothing; Germany's 0% needs a year of patience. The right one: 'Can I document why my activity is investing, not trading?'
items.tweetB: Germany's 0% after 12 months is the single biggest retail tax carve-out in crypto and the author flags a high risk it gets reformed. If that goes, the 'hold for a year' behaviour it created goes with it. Watch $BTC holder cohort behaviour.

items.title: DAC8: EU crypto reporting applies to 2026 activity, first reports in 2027
items.idea: The author notes EU DAC8 reporting rules apply to reportable activity from 2026 with initial reporting in 2027 under national implementations, and stresses tax-free treatment and reporting obligations are separate questions.
items.angle: Zero-tax jurisdictions do not mean zero visibility; relevant to CEX/custody compliance flows and to self-custody demand.
items.tweetA: Low tax is not low visibility. DAC8 means EU exchanges report your 2026 activity to your tax authority in 2027 regardless of where you moved your passport. The 'quiet exit' trade has a paper trail.
items.tweetB: The first DAC8 reports land in 2027 on 2026 activity. Expect a wave of retroactive compliance spending at exchanges and a quiet bid for self-custody tooling. $COIN
